items.title: Sunset and Holloway
items.text:
First came the smell of incense. Quiet mantras muted by angled necks between wood. A bullish young woman with duck feet walked past aisle right and exited beneath green. From behind, a man whispered Irish. Veils covered pupils.

Technicolor.

A man stood before the crowd, naked, laden in gold, his features impossible to collect.

An older woman, not a sailor, patrolled the perimeter wearing a white ruffled button-up shirt, black silk vest, black pleated trousers, and leather riding boots. Her tussled hair was bleached and curled, revealing Chanel earrings.

"Tom, Tom, Tom, Tom, Tom, Tom, Tom."

From her mouth, the name changed pitch with each quiet shriek, the Doppler effect exaggerated by the otherwise silent room.

I shut my eyes.

Darkness has geometry. Friction of clothes. A throat cleared. Beads collided in someone's hand. Somewhere, a dog barked in polyrhythm. The room redrew itself through echolocation. I learned the tongue-click method in college from a blind man named Binááʼ Ádaadinígíí, whom I called B.A. He was thirty-three, finishing his bachelor's degree. B.A. taught me to hear walls before seeing them. He also taught me violence, regret, and anguish, though not necessarily in that order. I clicked once against the roof of my mouth. The room returned.

Power, glory, blessings, forgiveness. I asked for all of it.

The naked man remained impossible to read.

A phantom dizziness suggested I was on a boat. Footsteps gave way to increasing silence. Then something cold wrapped itself around my patellas before slipping down my calves and back across my feet. Audible gasps arrived sequentially as the cold spread from the north side of the room toward the southwest. I refused to open my eyes. The cold climbed my quadriceps, threatening to impair my Micro Maestro™, which was not named for its size but—

I opened them.

Water covered the floor and continued rising.

The naked man remained unaffected. I could finally distinguish a smile. His colors pulsed with impossible saturation. Yes! He was looking directly at me.

The water reached my chest. I unfolded my hands and gripped the wooden crest rail.

His lips began to parse.

My name.

"Wreeeeeeoooooowww..."

"Rwoooooeeeeeeooooowww..."

A nearby fire department siren denatured the sweetness of his words. Son of a bitch.

I looked away, if only for a moment.

When I looked back he was gone.

Body trembling, clothes soaked, I stood and followed the current to the street.

Outside it was eighty-eight degrees and cloudless. Sunset and Holloway. The sun sat above a billboard's turned-up nose. Every business was televising the World Cup. There were screams that sounded like cheers, and cheers that sounded like screams. A gaping hole had opened in the Boulevard. Water erupted from a broken main.

Nobody seemed to notice.

items.title: Untitled 1
items.text:
There’s a man I pass on my way to the store. He lies beneath the palm tree at the park. The park was once overrun with homeless people, but now it’s just him.

He rests his head on a 1.5-liter bottle of soda, upside down, so the mouth of the bottle digs into the ground and the wide grooves at the base nest into his occipital. The hill has just enough slope that his heels anchor his body to the shade.

The bottle is dollar store root beer, almost identical to one I remember from 2004. It sat quietly inside the GE fridge while the television said the same company had found its way into operations in Iraq. There was a war going on out there.

On the lawn: irrigating the property, pouring concrete, cleaning the job site, listening to Bill-E-Bob’s mania, brushing away the dog, Babette.

Steadfast.

Waiting.

Inside, the 1.5-liter bottle.

A prize of oil, refined into my saccharine celebration. It could be mixed with almost anything from Walmart. Especially ice cream. Two scoops of vanilla. The slow pour. Syrup crystallizing across the white. Then foam.

Military warhead explosions create temperatures high enough to turn desert sand into glass.

Desert.

Dessert.

There was a war going on out there.

items.title: Untitled 2
items.text:
Talkity talkity, talkity talkity, talkity talking,
Talkity talkity, talkity talking—talk radio.

Standing on the 8500 block of Santa Monica, looking between the oblong traffic light: the Healthy Spot, CVS, a KHY advertisement, Total Tan & Wellness Center, persons unknown, a vehicle speaking in other languages, a fleck of sunlight caught on the new apartments, Olive, Kings, Luchs, Crescent, another CVS, Yoko, Chateau, non-deciduous varieties, Stahl, Row, Eames, and directly through my Laurel Canyon Airbnb.

That is the eyeline of Mecca.

items.title: Untitled 3
items.text:
Madness awoke.
Madness arose.
Madness anointed the dust.
Madness composed.

What Madness had made
the surveyors named.

What Madness spoke
would tickle and fray.

Madness does hammer
the roads and the rails.

Madness did answer the call.
Madness entered by the narrow gate.

Madness in the rain.
Madness in the drain.
Madness under the tongue.

Madness did save the men on that day.

Madness laughed beneath the wires.
Madness caught lying.
Madness witnessed and was lost.

Madness drove home.
Singing that tune.
Singing that tune.
Singing that tune.

items.title: By Design
items.text:
By design they must have put him up front.

Every day we throw ourselves, unsettled, into the monotony and expect nothing but a miracle.
Parking validation. A receipt. A reflex to the query, unrequited.

Hair like mine but better. His face met itself like the sands of the beach. That is to say it was
perfect. His vascularity pulsed though no signs of peptides or gear announced themselves. It
was the type of beauty that asked a million questions.

I was the type of person who never asked.

But I was dying to.

I smoothly pressed my right index finger into the grocery store's biometric scanner, revealing my
shopping history, point accumulation and name.

Name.

I was dying to know his.

What is your name, sir?! By gosh, where are you from?!

The questions presented themselves and recoiled.

Instead I said,

"So you're an actor."

That seemed perfect. Confident. Relaxed. With a tinge of nonchalant interest.

Damn I'm good.

No.

I'm an idiot.

Like my phone background he could clearly see from its face-up position on the checkout
counter.

Idiot Shinji.

Idiot Noah.

He looked sad. The kind of somber that creates invisible turbulence. I could feel it and figured it
was my fault.

I hadn't shaved in two weeks. Though I'd walked nearly twelve miles a day for the last three
weeks, my thighs bulged from my baggy elastic suit pants, exasperated by the two anacondas
wrapped around them, squeezing in sync until the snakes and my own body became
indistinguishable. I also wore a white T-shirt that was too new.

I looked back up and fumbled for my debit card.

"Yes, I'll use my points."

"$62.97."

"Thank you very much."

"Sure thing."

I took the bags and walked away.

items.title: Whistlejacket
items.text:
No one talks about the sadness in his eyes.

The painting is usually discussed in terms of anatomy, musculature, breeding, or Stubbs’s extraordinary powers of observation. The horse is admired as an achievement before he is encountered as a subject. His scale encourages this. Standing before him, nearly life size, one is expected to surrender to magnificence.

Yet the expression resists the performance.

A once celebrated show horse has become a breeding animal. Stubbs removes almost everything that might distract from this fact. The landscape recedes until the body itself becomes the event. Rearing once more, he performs the gesture expected of him, but only for us. The pose survives the life that justified it.

His humiliation is permanent.

Millions pass before him. Every nationality. Every language. Increasingly, every visit concludes with a camera. We remember the horse by reproducing him. Not his sadness, but the institution that has successfully absorbed it into spectacle. Grandeur has a way of disguising grief.

The horse is not simply a victim of man’s domination of nature. He is a victim of what history asks monuments to become. His body no longer belongs to the field, nor even to Stubbs. It belongs to remembrance itself. He exists to certify a version of greatness whose original conditions have long since disappeared.

Photography performs a curious labour here. Barthes described the photograph as the that-has-been: a technology that certifies presence while simultaneously announcing its loss. Before Stubbs’s horse, the phone becomes less an instrument of memory than of postponement. We photograph what we cannot yet fully absorb. The image enters the archive where it waits until the feeling attached to it becomes bearable.

Instagram story. Wine bar. Highly rated gelato. The Underground. Two in the morning, unable to sleep.

The horse remains where he has always been.

It’s possible that no one speaks of the sadness in his eyes because doing so would require admitting that we recognise it immediately. We come to remember greatness. Instead, we encounter the afterlife of it.
